title: Rhetorical Synthesis
what_is_tested: These questions give you a student's research notes and a writing goal, and test whether you can pick the sentence that uses the notes to meet that goal. Every choice is accurate, so the skill is matching purpose, not checking facts.
how_to_spot: A list of bulleted notes appears with no passage, and the question begins "The student wants to..." and asks which choice "most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal."
method: Read the question first, before the notes, and underline the goal's key words (for example "difference," "similarity," "introduce," "aim and method," "generalization").
Note any audience in the goal; an "unfamiliar" audience needs a basic explanation of what something is.
Skim the notes only to see which facts would serve that goal.
Check each choice against the goal, not against the notes; every choice will be true.
Make sure the choice does every part of the goal, such as both items in a comparison.
pitfalls: Choosing the longest choice or the one with the most facts instead of the one that meets the goal (misses the goal).
Choosing a sentence that covers only half of a two-part goal, such as one item in a comparison (too narrow).
Choosing an accurate fact from the notes that is unrelated to the goal (true but irrelevant).
Reading the notes carefully before the goal, which wastes time and makes every fact seem important.
Forgetting the audience: for an unfamiliar audience, a sentence that assumes the reader already knows the subject misses the goal.

cards.title: Foundations: underline the goal
steps: Read the goal first and underline its key word, such as "difference" or "similarity."
For a difference or similarity, look for a choice that mentions both things being compared.
Check that the choice actually shows the difference or similarity, often with words like "while," "whereas," "both," or "like."
Ignore whether a choice is interesting or detailed; ask only whether it does the goal.

notes: The Thar Desert lies in northwestern India and southeastern Pakistan.
The Sahara stretches across much of North Africa.
It covers about 9 million square kilometers, making it the largest hot desert in the world.
worked_example.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference in size between the two deserts. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The Thar Desert, which covers about 200,000 square kilometers, lies in northwestern India and southeastern Pakistan.
choices.B: The Sahara, which stretches across much of North Africa, is the largest hot desert in the world.
choices.C: The Thar Desert covers about 200,000 square kilometers, while the Sahara covers about 9 million square kilometers.
choices.D: The Thar Desert lies in South Asia, and the Sahara stretches across much of North Africa.

walkthrough: The goal's key words are "difference in size between the two deserts."
So the sentence must give a size for both deserts and set them side by side.
C gives both areas joined by "while," which shows the difference, so it is correct.
D is the trap because it mentions both deserts, but it compares their locations, not their sizes.

cards.title: Medium: writing for an unfamiliar audience
steps: When the goal mentions an audience "unfamiliar" with the subject, the sentence must explain what the subject is.
Look for a choice that names the subject and gives a short description (what kind of thing it is, where it comes from).
Reject choices that assume the reader already knows the subject, even if they contain impressive facts.
Confirm that the choice still matches any other part of the goal.

notes: Jamdani is a traditional weaving technique from Bangladesh.
It produces fine, lightweight cotton cloth, often used for saris.
Weavers add the patterns by hand while the cloth is being woven on a loom, rather than printing or stitching them on afterward.
In 2013, UNESCO added the traditional art of jamdani weaving to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage.
worked_example.stem: The student wants to introduce jamdani to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In 2013, UNESCO added the traditional art of jamdani weaving to its list of intangible cultural heritage.
choices.B: Jamdani, a traditional weaving technique from Bangladesh, produces fine cotton cloth with patterns woven in by hand on the loom.
choices.C: Jamdani patterns are added by hand during weaving rather than printed or stitched on afterward.
choices.D: Fine, lightweight jamdani cloth is often used to make saris.

walkthrough: The goal is to "introduce" jamdani to readers who have never heard of it.
Such readers first need to know what jamdani is and where it comes from.
B says it is a weaving technique from Bangladesh and briefly describes the cloth, so it introduces the subject.
A is the strongest trap: the UNESCO fact is impressive, but it never tells an unfamiliar reader what jamdani actually is.

cards.title: Advanced: aim, method, or finding?
steps: For a study, sort the notes into three labels: aim (what the researcher wanted to know), method (what was done), and finding (what was found).
Underline which of those labels the goal asks for; it may ask for two of them.
Check each choice for exactly those parts; a choice with the wrong pair misses the goal.
Do not reward a choice for including extra background that the goal does not ask for.

notes: Eurasian blackbirds usually begin singing shortly before dawn.
Ecologist Mei Lin Chou wanted to know whether artificial light at night affects when city blackbirds start their morning song.
Her team placed sound recorders at 12 sites in one city, each with a different level of night lighting.
Blackbirds at the most brightly lit sites began singing about 40 minutes earlier than those at the darkest sites.
worked_example.stem: The student wants to present the aim and the finding of Chou's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Chou's team placed sound recorders at 12 city sites with different levels of night lighting to study blackbirds.
choices.B: Eurasian blackbirds usually begin singing shortly before dawn, and Chou's team recorded them at 12 sites.
choices.C: Chou wanted to know whether artificial light at night affects when city blackbirds start their morning song, so her team placed sound recorders at 12 sites.
choices.D: Investigating whether artificial light at night affects when city blackbirds start singing, Chou found that birds at the brightest sites began about 40 minutes earlier than those at the darkest sites.

walkthrough: The notes contain an aim (note 2), a method (note 3), and a finding (note 4); the goal asks for the aim and the finding.
D states the question Chou investigated and the 40-minute result.
So D meets both parts of the goal.
C is the near miss: it gives the aim but pairs it with the method, so the finding, which the goal requires, is missing.

cards.title: Challenge: goals with a built-in contrast
steps: Underline every part of the goal, including words like "unusual," "challenge," or "compared with."
Find the note that supplies the background or expectation and the note that supplies the surprise.
Choose the sentence that puts both together, usually with "although," "unlike," or "while."
Reject choices that report the surprising fact alone; without the background, the contrast the goal asks for is missing.

notes: Bar-tailed godwits are shorebirds that breed in Alaska and spend the northern winter in Australia and New Zealand.
Most migrating birds stop several times along the way to rest and feed.
Godwits cannot rest on the ocean's surface.
In 2022, a five-month-old godwit fitted with a tracking tag flew from Alaska to Tasmania, Australia, without stopping.
The flight covered about 13,560 kilometers and took about 11 days.
worked_example.stem: The student wants to emphasize how unusual the young godwit's flight was compared with the journeys of most migrating birds. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Unlike most migrating birds, which stop several times to rest and feed, a young bar-tailed godwit flew about 13,560 kilometers from Alaska to Tasmania without stopping.
choices.B: In 2022, a five-month-old bar-tailed godwit flew from Alaska to Tasmania, a journey of about 13,560 kilometers that took about 11 days.
choices.C: Bar-tailed godwits, which cannot rest on the ocean's surface, breed in Alaska and spend the northern winter in Australia and New Zealand.
choices.D: A young bar-tailed godwit wearing a tracking tag flew for about 11 days in 2022, traveling from Alaska to Tasmania, Australia.

walkthrough: The goal has two parts: show the flight was unusual and compare it with "most migrating birds."
The comparison comes from note 2 (most birds stop) and the surprise from notes 4 and 5 (nonstop, 13,560 kilometers).
A joins them with "Unlike," so it meets the whole goal.
B is the most attractive trap because its numbers are impressive, but it never mentions other birds, so the comparison is missing.
